facts.statement: Fossils of Coccosteus have been found throughout Europe and North America.
facts.quote: Its fossils have been found throughout Europe and North America.

facts.statement: Most Coccosteus fossils are found in freshwater sediments, suggesting the animal may have occasionally entered saltwater.
facts.quote: The majority of these have been found in freshwater sediments, though such a large range suggests that they may have been able to enter saltwater.

facts.statement: Coccosteus was a small placoderm, with the species C. cuspidatus measuring between 29.6 and 39.4 cm in length.
facts.quote: It was a small placoderm, with Coccosteus cuspidatus measuring 29.6 - 39.4 cm long.

facts.statement: Coccosteus possessed a joint between the armor of its body and skull, a trait shared with other arthrodires.
facts.quote: Like all other arthrodires, Coccosteus had a joint between the armor of the body and skull.

facts.statement: Coccosteus could feed on fairly large prey due to its longer jaws and wide-opening mouth.
facts.quote: Along with the longer jaws, this allowed Coccosteus to feed on fairly large prey.

facts.statement: The up-and-down movement of Coccosteus's skull allowed more water to be pumped through its gills.
facts.quote: The up-and-down movement of the skull also allowed for more water to be pumped through the gills.

facts.statement: Researchers suggest Coccosteus may have supplemented its diet by filtering organic material from mud using its gills.
facts.quote: Possibly, the creature supplemented its diet with organic material filtered from mud using the gills.

facts.statement: Coccosteus kept its beak sharp by having the edges of its dental plates grind against each other.
facts.quote: The beak was kept sharp by having the edges of the dental plates grind away at each other.

facts.statement: Coccosteus looked similar to the giant Dunkleosteus, but its eyes were positioned closer to the end of its snout.
facts.quote: Overall the creature looked similar to its gigantic cousin Dunkleosteus, save that its eyes were closer to the end of its snout than in its larger relative.

facts.statement: Coccosteus is the type genus for the family Coccosteidae, which belongs to the clade Coccosteomorphi within Eubrachythoraci.
facts.quote: Coccosteus is the type genus for family Coccosteidae, which belongs to the clade Coccosteomorphi, one of the two major clades within Eubrachythoraci.

facts.statement: The genus Coccosteus was described by Agassiz in 1843.
Coccosteus lived during the Middle to Late Devonian periods.
C. cuspidatus is the type species of Coccosteus and serves as an important index fossil in the Devonian sequence of northern Scotland's Orcadian Basin.
facts.quote: C. cuspidatus is the type species, and is an important index fossil in the continental Devonian sequence of northern Scotland deposited in the Orcadian Basin.

facts.statement: The genus Coccosteus was originally described by Agassiz in 1841.
The largest Coccosteus specimens measured about 40 cm, while the average length was between 20 and 24 cm.
facts.quote: Los ejemplares más grandes midieron unos 40 cm, aunque la longitud media fue de 20 a 24 cm.

facts.statement: Coccosteus, likely the best-known arthrodire, was described in 1841, and up to 49 species have been identified since, many later reclassified.
facts.quote: Probablemente el artrodiro mejor conocido, Coccosteus fue descrito en 1841, y desde entonces se han identificado hasta 49 especies, muchas de ellas reclasificadas posteriormente.

facts.statement: Coccosteus lived from the Emsian to the Famennian stages, between 410.62 and 358.86 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Emsian to Famennian (410.62 to 358.86 million years ago)
